name: Faience making in the Near East and Egypt
summary: Faience, a glazed body of crushed quartz, first appeared at the end of the fifth millennium BCE, perhaps in the Near East, and was perfected in Egypt.
description: Faience is a man-made material: a core of crushed quartz bound by a little soda-lime-silicate glass under a bright glaze, usually blue. The Met essay says it first appeared at the end of the fifth millennium BCE, may have been invented in the ancient Near East following the alkaline glazing of quartz stones, and was refined in Egypt, where beads were among the earliest objects.

impact.note: Faience beads, amulets and vessels were made throughout Egypt and the Near East for millennia (most of one civilisation, for generations) as a cheaper stand-in for rare blue stones, an improvement not a new way of life; the later vitreous materials, glass and ceramic glazes, are generally held to rest on it, which is recalled and not shown by the cited essay.

date.label: end of the fifth millennium BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Faience first appeared at the end of the fifth millennium BCE and may have been invented in the ancient Near East.

evidence.supports: Faience first appeared at the end of the fifth millennium B.C. and has occurred in various forms up to the present day. It may have been invented in the ancient Near East

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Read Tite and Shortland, Production Technology of Faience and Related Early Vitreous Materials (2008), for the excavated finds behind the date and for the priority of the Near East or Egypt, including glazed steatite.
Date the glazed quartz stones and glazed steatite that the essay places before faience; they belong to this concept and may move the earliest date back.
The years -4100 to -4000 are a conversion of the Met's words 'end of the fifth millennium', not a range from the source; check against the primary excavation dates.
Trace the evidenced connection from faience to the first glass and to glazed pottery, on which the generativity score depends.

research.note: The record stands for the earliest glazing tradition: the Met essay dates the first appearance of faience anywhere to the end of the fifth millennium BCE, which is the dated marker here, while the alkaline glazing of quartz stones that it says came before is not dated in this source; whether the Near East or Egypt came first is left open.
